meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 2: Architecture & Components

questions.question: In MCP's architecture, what is the role of the 'MCP Host'?

options.text: The program that provides context data to clients
The AI application that coordinates and manages one or multiple MCP clients
The transport layer that frames JSON-RPC messages
The authorization server that issues tokens

questions.explanation: The MCP host is the AI application (e.g., Claude Desktop, VS Code) that coordinates and manages MCP clients. Each client maintains a dedicated connection to one MCP server, and servers provide context to clients.

questions.question: How many MCP servers does a single MCP client connect to?

options.text: Exactly one — each client maintains a dedicated connection to one server
Up to ten servers per client
As many servers as the host configures
Two: one local and one remote

questions.explanation: The host creates one MCP client for each MCP server it connects to. Each client maintains a dedicated one-to-one connection with its corresponding server.

questions.question: Which two transport mechanisms does MCP support?

options.text: WebSocket and gRPC
Stdio and Streamable HTTP
TCP sockets and GraphQL
MQTT and Server-Sent Events only

questions.explanation: MCP supports the stdio transport (standard input/output for local processes) and the Streamable HTTP transport (HTTP POST with optional Server-Sent Events, used for remote servers).

questions.question: What underlying RPC protocol does MCP's data layer use?

options.text: gRPC
SOAP
JSON-RPC 2.0
REST over HTTP/2

questions.explanation: The data layer implements a JSON-RPC 2.0 based exchange protocol that defines message structure and semantics, and the same JSON-RPC format is used across all transports.

questions.question: As of protocol version 2026-07-28, MCP is described as a stateless protocol. What does this mean in practice?

options.text: Servers never store any data anywhere
Every request carries the protocol version and relevant capabilities in its _meta field, so servers can process each request on its own
Clients must reconnect after every request
Notifications are no longer supported

questions.explanation: Statelessness means each request is self-contained: the _meta field carries io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and clientCapabilities (and normally clientInfo), so the server infers nothing from previous requests.

questions.question: Which request lets a client learn a server's supported protocol versions, capabilities, and identity in a single call?

options.text: initialize
server/discover
capabilities/get
server/handshake

questions.explanation: The mandatory server/discover request returns supportedVersions, the server's capabilities object, and serverInfo in _meta. Calling it is optional for clients, since every request already carries per-request metadata, but every server must implement it.

questions.question: How does a client opt in to receiving change notifications (such as tool list changes) from a server in protocol version 2026-07-28?

options.text: Notifications are always sent automatically to every connected client
The client polls notifications/poll every few seconds
The client opens a long-lived subscriptions/listen stream naming the notification types it wants
The client sets a webhook URL during initialization

questions.explanation: Change notifications are opt-in: the client sends a subscriptions/listen request with a notifications filter (e.g., toolsListChanged: true). The server acknowledges with notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged and delivers matching notifications on that stream.

questions.question: In a subscriptions/listen flow, what value does the io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId field in each notification's _meta carry?

options.text: A random UUID generated per notification
The JSON-RPC ID of the subscriptions/listen request that opened the stream
The server's version string
A monotonically increasing sequence number

questions.explanation: Every notification on the stream carries a subscriptionId equal to the JSON-RPC ID of the subscriptions/listen request that opened it, letting clients correlate notifications with the subscription that produced them.

questions.question: What guarantee does MCP make about delivery of change notifications?

options.text: Exactly-once delivery is guaranteed
At-least-once delivery is guaranteed
Delivery is best effort; clients should also rely on polling to preserve freshness
Notifications are retried indefinitely until acknowledged

questions.explanation: Notifications are best effort — there is no guarantee every notification is sent or received, particularly across transport reconnects, so clients should also poll to keep results fresh.

questions.question: Which statement about local vs remote MCP servers is correct?

options.text: Local servers typically use the STDIO transport and serve a single client, while remote servers typically use Streamable HTTP and serve many clients
Local servers must use HTTP; remote servers must use STDIO
Remote servers cannot expose tools, only resources
A server's location changes its protocol semantics

questions.explanation: 'MCP server' refers to the program serving context regardless of where it runs. Local servers use STDIO and typically serve one client; remote servers use Streamable HTTP and typically serve many clients. The data layer semantics stay the same.

questions.question: In the 2026-07-28 spec, what are the ttlMs and cacheScope fields returned in results like server/discover and tools/list used for?

options.text: Rate limiting the client's requests
Caching: ttlMs is a freshness hint in milliseconds and cacheScope indicates who may reuse the response
Timing out slow tool calls
Configuring the transport keep-alive interval

questions.explanation: Results carry caching hints: ttlMs tells the client how long the result stays fresh (e.g., a tool list cacheable for five minutes), and cacheScope indicates who may reuse it (e.g., public). A cached list should also be treated as stale once a list_changed notification arrives.

questions.question: According to the specification overview, MCP takes inspiration from which existing protocol?

options.text: The Language Server Protocol (LSP)
The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP)

questions.explanation: The spec notes that MCP takes inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which standardized language support across development tools; MCP similarly standardizes integrating context and tools into AI applications.

questions.question: What is the authoritative source of truth for the MCP specification's protocol requirements?

options.text: The TypeScript schema (schema.ts) in the specification repository
A PDF published annually
The Python SDK source code
The MCP Inspector's behavior

questions.explanation: The specification defines the authoritative protocol requirements based on the TypeScript schema in schema.ts for each protocol version (e.g., schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts).

questions.question: SCENARIO: A client sends a request declaring protocol version 2026-07-28 in _meta, but the server only supports 2025-11-25. What happens according to the discovery/versioning model?

options.text: The server silently downgrades and answers in the older format
The server rejects the request with an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError listing the versions it supports, and the client retries with a mutually supported version
The transport connection is terminated with no explanation
The server forwards the request to a newer server

questions.explanation: If a server doesn't support the requested version, it rejects the request with an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError (-32022) whose data lists supported versions; the client can then retry with a version both sides support. server/discover's supportedVersions lets clients learn this up front.

questions.question: How do the data layer and transport layer relate conceptually in MCP?

options.text: The data layer is the inner layer (JSON-RPC protocol, primitives) and the transport layer is the outer layer (connections, framing, authorization)
They are the same layer viewed from different sides
The transport layer defines tools; the data layer defines HTTP headers
The data layer only exists for stdio servers

questions.explanation: Conceptually the data layer (JSON-RPC 2.0 exchange, discovery, primitives, notifications) is the inner layer, wrapped by the transport layer (stdio or Streamable HTTP), which handles connection establishment, message framing, and authorization while keeping the same JSON-RPC format everywhere.

questions.question: SCENARIO: An MCP host connects to 3 different MCP servers, and one of those servers (a remote one) also serves 50 other users' hosts. Describe the cardinality correctly.

options.text: The host instantiates 3 MCP clients — one per server, each holding a dedicated 1:1 connection; the remote server meanwhile serves many clients (one per connected host)
One client multiplexes all 3 servers
Each server requires 3 clients
Hosts connect to servers directly without clients

questions.explanation: Cardinality: Host → many clients; each client ↔ exactly one server (dedicated connection). Local STDIO servers typically serve a single client, while remote Streamable HTTP servers typically serve many clients across hosts.

questions.question: How does Streamable HTTP differ from the legacy HTTP+SSE transport it replaced?

options.text: They are identical apart from the name

Legacy HTTP+SSE used separate endpoints (a long-lived GET/SSE channel plus a POST endpoint); Streamable HTTP (introduced 2025-03-26) uses a single MCP endpoint where POST carries client messages with optional SSE streaming on the response — and HTTP+SSE is now formally Deprecated
Streamable HTTP requires WebSockets
HTTP+SSE was faster and remains recommended

questions.explanation: Streamable HTTP replaced the two-endpoint HTTP+SSE design with a single endpoint supporting POST plus optional SSE streaming. The 2026-07-28 revision reclassified HTTP+SSE as Deprecated under the lifecycle policy, with migration to Streamable HTTP.

questions.question: How does capability negotiation differ between the legacy and modern protocol eras?

options.text: There is no capability negotiation in either era

Legacy (≤2025-11-25): capabilities are exchanged once in the initialize handshake and apply to the whole session. Modern (2026-07-28): negotiation is per-request — the client declares clientCapabilities in every request's _meta, and the server's capabilities are discoverable via server/discover
Capabilities are negotiated in DNS TXT records
Only servers declare capabilities; clients never do

questions.explanation: Capability negotiation ensures unsupported operations are never attempted. Legacy sessions negotiated once at initialize; the stateless modern era moved this to per-request metadata plus the mandatory server/discover RPC, and MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError (-32021) fires when a needed client capability wasn't declared.

questions.question: SCENARIO: In the docs' example, Visual Studio Code connects to the Sentry MCP server and then also to the local filesystem server. What happens inside VS Code?

options.text: One shared client object handles both servers
The VS Code runtime (the host) instantiates one MCP client object per connection — a second client is created for the filesystem server, each maintaining its own dedicated connection
Sentry proxies the filesystem traffic
VS Code must restart between servers

questions.explanation: This example illustrates the participant model: VS Code acts as the MCP host; connecting to each additional server instantiates an additional MCP client object dedicated to that server.

questions.question: In the 2026-07-28 revision, what replaced the initialize/notifications/initialized handshake?

options.text: A new handshake/start method that must be called once per connection
Every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta; server/discover is available for up-front discovery
An HTTP-only Mcp-Session-Id header that carries the negotiated capabilities
A TLS extension that embeds the protocol version in the certificate

questions.explanation: SEP-2575 removed the handshake entirely. Each request self-describes via _meta (io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and clientCapabilities), and clients MAY call server/discover for up-front version/capability discovery. (Spec 2026-07-28 changelog, major change 2-3.)

questions.question: Which _meta fields are REQUIRED on every client request in protocol version 2026-07-28?

options.text: io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, clientCapabilities, and clientInfo
io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion and clientCapabilities only
io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo and clientCapabilities only
io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion only

questions.explanation: protocolVersion and clientCapabilities are required on every request. clientInfo is a SHOULD (recommended but optional), and logLevel is optional. A common trap is treating clientInfo as required. (Spec basic/index, per-request protocol fields table.)

questions.question: A request arrives missing the required io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities _meta field. What must the server return?

options.text: -32021 MissingRequiredClientCapability
-32602 Invalid params, and on HTTP a 400 Bad Request status
-32600 Invalid request, and on HTTP a 401 status
It should process the request assuming empty capabilities

questions.explanation: A request missing a required _meta field is malformed: the server MUST reject it with -32602 (Invalid params) and HTTP 400. -32021 is different: it applies when the fields are present but a needed capability was not declared. (Spec basic/index.)

questions.question: A client's request includes valid _meta, but processing it requires a capability the client did not declare in clientCapabilities. What does the spec require?

options.text: The server proceeds and hopes the client can handle the response
The server returns -32602 Invalid params
The server returns MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError (-32021) with data.requiredCapabilities listing what is missing, HTTP 400
The server silently downgrades to a reduced feature set

questions.explanation: A server MUST NOT rely on capabilities the client has not declared. If a needed capability is absent, it MUST return -32021 with data.requiredCapabilities listing the missing capabilities (HTTP 400). (Spec basic/index.)

questions.question: Which statement about server/discover is correct in 2026-07-28?

options.text: Clients MUST call it before any other request
Servers MUST implement it; clients MAY call it (e.g., for up-front version selection or as a stdio backward-compatibility probe)
It is optional for servers but mandatory for clients on stdio
It replaces tools/list, prompts/list, and resources/list

questions.explanation: Servers MUST implement server/discover, but calling it is optional for clients - a client can invoke any RPC inline and handle UnsupportedProtocolVersionError. It is useful for presenting server info in one request and as the stdio legacy-vs-modern probe. (Spec server/discover.)

questions.question: Which set of information does a server/discover result carry?

options.text: supportedVersions, capabilities (including extensions), serverInfo in _meta, optional instructions, plus ttlMs and cacheScope
Only supportedVersions and a session token
The complete tools, prompts, and resources catalogs
The server's OAuth client_id and scopes_supported

questions.explanation: DiscoverResult includes supportedVersions, capabilities, _meta['io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo'], and optional instructions; the operation supports caching, so it also carries ttlMs and cacheScope. It does not return full primitive catalogs. (Spec server/discover.)

questions.question: A stdio server keeps a long-lived process per client and infers 'this connection already told me its capabilities' from an earlier request. Why does this violate 2026-07-28?

options.text: stdio servers must restart after each request
Servers MUST NOT rely on prior requests over the same connection for context; an open connection is not a session, and clients may interleave unrelated requests on one transport
Capabilities may only be transmitted over HTTP headers
It is allowed, as long as the process was launched by the client

questions.explanation: MCP is stateless: every request supplies its own metadata in _meta, and connection or process identity is explicitly not a proxy for session continuity. Cross-request state must use explicit identifiers passed on each request. (Spec basic/index, Statelessness.)

questions.question: A Streamable HTTP response stream breaks mid-request in the modern era. What must the client do?

options.text: Reconnect with the Last-Event-ID header to resume the stream
Send notifications/resume with the old request ID
Re-issue the lost request as a new request with a new request ID
Wait for the server to replay missed SSE events

questions.explanation: SSE resumability (Last-Event-ID and event IDs) was removed in 2026-07-28. A broken response stream loses the in-flight request; the client MUST re-issue it as a new request with a new ID. (Spec 2026-07-28 changelog, major change 9.)

questions.question: Which statement about the resultType field is FALSE under 2026-07-28?

options.text: A result with an unrecognized resultType value must be considered invalid by the client
Clients must treat an absent resultType from an earlier-protocol server as "complete"
Extensions may add resultType values, but only ones advertised via capabilities count as supported
A modern server may omit resultType on small results to save bytes

questions.explanation: Every result MUST include resultType in 2026-07-28 - there is no size exception. The other three statements are the exact spec rules: unrecognized values are invalid, absence from legacy servers means "complete", and extensions extend the value set via advertised capabilities. (Spec basic/index, ResultType.)

questions.question: Where does a modern server identify itself, and how much should clients trust that identity?

options.text: In io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo within each result's _meta (SHOULD); it is self-reported and must not drive security decisions
In a signed X-Server-Identity HTTP header that clients MUST verify
Only in the server/discover response; other results never carry identity
In the OAuth token's aud claim

questions.explanation: Servers SHOULD include io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo in every result's _meta. It is self-reported, intended for display/logging/debugging; implementations SHOULD NOT change behavior or make security decisions based on it. (Spec basic/index, per-response protocol fields.)
